title: Text
description: One prayer, blessing or poem with its word-by-word breakdown. Stored in processed/json/<id>.json.

id.description: Matches the file name, which is the input file's name: menucha_vsimcha for texts/menucha_vsimcha.txt.

title.description: The text's commonly used name, transliterated, e.g. "Menucha V'simcha". For part of a prayer: "Prayer: Part", e.g. "Havdala: Hinei El".

kind.description: poem: lines of verse. prose: continuous text.

sections.description: Natural divisions of the text: stanzas of a poem, paragraphs or blessings of prose. A text with no divisions has one section.

section.description: A refrain or other repeated stanza appears only once, where it first occurs; later repetitions are left out. It counts as a repetition only if its words are identical to the first occurrence (ignoring punctuation); if any word differs, it is a new section.

title.description: Name of the section, e.g. "Avot" or "V'ahavta". Given when the section has a commonly used name; left out otherwise, e.g. for the stanzas of a poem.

line.description: The smallest natural unit of the text: a verse of a poem, a pasuk, or a sentence of text that isn't a pasuk. A response added after a pasuk, such as כֵּן תִּהְיֶה לָּנוּ, is its own line.

hebrew.description: The full line, with nikud, keeping its punctuation, such as the sof pasuk ׃.

words.description: Words joined by a maqaf are separate words, each with its own root; the maqaf stays on the first: בְּכָל־לְבָבְךָ is בְּכָל־ (with all of) and לְבָבְךָ (your heart).

hebrew.description: The word as it appears in the line, without punctuation; a maqaf stays: מְאֹדֶךָ without the ׃ that ends its verse, בְּכָל־ with its maqaf.

meaning.description: Meaning of the word in this context.

phrase.description: A short phrase around the word, shown on its Anki cards instead of the whole line: the word with the words it belongs with, usually two or three words and at most four, such as its construct chain, a preposition with its noun, a verb with its subject or object, or a pair joined by ו. Copied from the line as it stands, a run of whole words that includes this word, without punctuation at either end: יְיָ אֱלֹהֵינוּ, בְּכָל־לְבָבְךָ, אָנֹכִי מְצַוְּךָ הַיּוֹם. Words that belong together share the same phrase. A short line can be its own phrase.

parts.description: Prefixes, base word and suffixes, in order, each with its meaning in context. A single entry if the word is not split. Keep the ל of an infinitive with its verb: לְאַמֵּץ (to strengthen) is one infinitive-construct part. A preposition with a merged article is one preposition part with "the" in its meaning: לַ־ (for the). A plural noun with a pronoun suffix splits into its construct plural and the full plural suffix, so the shared letters appear in both: אֱלֹהֵינוּ (our God) is אֱלֹהֵי (God of) and ־ֵינוּ (our).

root.description: Key into processed/json/roots.json. The commonly taught root of the word, whenever there is one. Left out only for words with no commonly taught root. When it's unclear whether a root is commonly taught, keep it if it links the word to other words in the siddur or the Torah; otherwise leave it out. Even then, leave out a root that would point to an unrelated meaning. Names follow the same rule.

part.description: One component of a word. Store every grammatical fact the Hebrew marks; outputs decide which ones to print and how to label them.

hebrew.description: Prefixes end with a maqaf and suffixes start with one: וְ־ (and), ־ָיו (his). A base word is written as it stands on its own, undoing changes caused by its prefixes and suffixes (dagesh, vowels, endings); a noun or verb that takes a suffix keeps its construct form. E.g. יְהוּדִים in לַיְּהוּדִים, כָּל־ in וּבְכָל־, שֶׁבֶת in בְּשִׁבְתְּךָ, אֶל־ in אֵלָיו.

meaning.description: A part in construct ends in "of": יוֹם (day of), מַלְכוּת (kingdom of) in מַלְכוּתוֹ.

pos.description: Particles are words that fit no other part of speech, such as the relative אֲשֶׁר (that), the object marker אֵת, הִנֵּה (behold) and סֶלָה (Selah); the object marker's meaning is "(marks the direct object)".

type.description: Kind of pronoun; only on pos pronoun. Pronoun suffixes are always personal.

form.description: After a vav that flips the tense, the verb keeps its written form, past or future, and its meaning shows the flipped tense: וַיְהִי (and He became) is future, וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם (and you shall draw) is past. Present and participle are the same Hebrew form (beinoni); choose by how the word functions. present: the verb of its clause, e.g. מְעִידִים (they testify). participle: works as a noun or adjective (takes the article הַ, is in construct, describes a noun, or means "one who…"), e.g. גּוֹאֵל (redeemer), מִתְעַנְּגִים in הַמִּתְעַנְּגִים (who delight). passive-participle: every passive form (the קָטוּל pattern, Pu'al/Hof'al מְ־/מֻ־ forms) whatever its function, e.g. בְּרוּאִים (created).

construct.description: True if the word is in construct (smichut) form. Also true for a noun or participle with a pronoun suffix, since the suffix attaches to the construct form.

pattern.description: The template from grammar/nouns.md the noun is built with, when it has one; only on nouns. mem-prefix: a מ that isn't a root letter, e.g. מִצְוָה (commandment), מָרוֹם (height). tav-prefix: a ת that isn't a root letter, e.g. תְּפִלָּה (prayer). hei-ending: a kubutz or shuruk before the last root letter and a feminine ending, e.g. יְשׁוּעָה (salvation), also in construct and plural: יְשׁוּעַת, יְשׁוּעוֹת. vav-tav-ending: a וּת ending that isn't a root letter, e.g. מַלְכוּת (kingdom). dagesh-vav: a hiriq under the first root letter, a dagesh in the second and וּ before the last, with no ending, e.g. קִדּוּשׁ (sanctification). A noun with a מ or ת prefix takes that pattern even if it also has an ending, e.g. מְנוּחָה (rest) is mem-prefix. Left out for nouns that are only a root with vowels, such as דֶּרֶךְ, or have only a plain feminine ending, such as שִׂמְחָה.

language.description: Language of the part when it isn't Hebrew; left out for Hebrew. Mark a part only when its form belongs to the other language: prefixes shared by Hebrew and Aramaic (וְ־, בְּ־, לְ־) follow the language of the surrounding text. E.g. רַבָּה (great), דְּ־ (of) and the ending ־ָא (the) are Aramaic.

allOf.description: Only verbs have binyan and form; verbs must have both.
Only pronouns have a type; pronouns must have one.
Personal pronouns and pronoun suffixes have person and number (gender is required except in 1st person, see below).
2nd and 3rd person personal pronouns and pronoun suffixes have gender.
Demonstratives have gender and number but no person ("common" gender for אֵלֶּה).
Interrogatives have no person, gender or number.
Nouns and adjectives always have gender and number.
Past and future verbs have person and number (gender is required except in 1st person, see below).
2nd and 3rd person past and future verbs have gender.
Imperatives are 2nd person with gender and number.
Present tense and participles have gender and number but no person.
Infinitives have no person, gender or number.
1st person has no gender in Hebrew.

root.description: 3 or 4 Hebrew letters separated by hyphens, e.g. "ש-מ-ר". Only the last letter may be a final form, and it must be one where it exists ("ל-א-ך", not "ל-א-כ"), so each root has exactly one spelling.
